title: LINQ in depth
lesson:
In Level 1 you met `Where`, `Select` and `Sum`. Now that you know lambdas are just functions passed as values, LINQ makes full sense: every LINQ method takes a lambda that says **what** you want, and LINQ does the looping.

The ones you'll use every week:

```
harvests.Where(h => h.Kg > 20)                 // keep some
        .Select(h => h.Farmer)                 // turn each into something else
        .Distinct()                            // drop repeats
        .OrderBy(name => name)                 // sort (OrderByDescending for high first)
        .ToList();                             // run it and make a list
```

- **Sorting by two things:** `.OrderByDescending(s => s.Points).ThenBy(s => s.Player)`. Use `ThenBy`, not a second `OrderBy`: a second OrderBy throws away the first sort.
- **Totals:** `Sum`, `Average`, `Min`, `Max`, `Count`, each with an optional lambda: `harvests.Sum(h => h.Kg)`.
- **Questions:** `Any(s => s.Points > 100)` (at least one?) and `All(...)` (every one?).
- **Picking one:** `First(...)` throws if nothing matches; `FirstOrDefault(...)` gives null (or 0) instead. Use FirstOrDefault when "none" is a normal answer.

**GroupBy** is the report-maker. It splits items into buckets by a key, and each bucket has a `Key` and the items in it:

```
var perFarmer = harvests
    .GroupBy(h => h.Farmer)
    .Select(g => new { Farmer = g.Key, Kg = g.Sum(h => h.Kg) })
    .OrderByDescending(t => t.Kg)
    .ToList();
```

That's "total kilograms per farmer, biggest first" in five lines. The `new { ... }` is an **anonymous type**: a quick record with no class needed.

**Common mistakes:**
- `Average()` on an empty list throws. Check `Any()` first, or decide what "no data" should return.
- LINQ is **lazy**: a query isn't run until you loop over it or call `ToList()`, `Sum()`, `First()`... If the list changes in between, you get the new answer. Call `ToList()` when you want a fixed snapshot.
- Don't chain so much that nobody can read it. Break long queries into named steps.

In games LINQ is great for menus, leaderboards, loot tables and save files. Inside Unity's `Update()`, which runs every frame, prefer plain loops for hot code, because LINQ creates small objects that the garbage collector must clean up.

notes: Sum takes a lambda that says which number to add up.
Any asks 'at least one?'; All asks 'every one?'.
GroupBy makes buckets; g.Key is the crop, and g holds that crop's harvests.
ThenBy breaks ties without undoing the first sort.
FirstOrDefault returns null instead of throwing when nothing matches.

exercises.title: Harvest report
exercises.prompt:
Harvest is given. In static class Report, using LINQ:
- int TotalKg(List<Harvest> h, string crop): total kg of that crop (crop names match ignoring case).
- List<string> Farmers(List<Harvest> h): each farmer once, A to Z.
- string BestCrop(List<Harvest> h): the crop with the most kg in total (ties: alphabetical first), or "none" for an empty list.
- List<string> Totals(List<Harvest> h): one line per farmer like "Amina: 70", highest total first, ties A to Z.

tests.call: Report.TotalKg(new List<Harvest> { new("Amina", "maize", 40), new("Juma", "beans", 25), new("Amina", "beans", 30), new("Wanjiru", "maize", 55), new("Juma", "maize", 10) }, "Maize")
tests.name: total of one crop

tests.call: Report.Farmers(new List<Harvest> { new("Amina", "maize", 40), new("Juma", "beans", 25), new("Amina", "beans", 30), new("Wanjiru", "maize", 55), new("Juma", "maize", 10) })
tests.name: farmers once each

tests.call: Report.BestCrop(new List<Harvest> { new("Amina", "maize", 40), new("Juma", "beans", 25), new("Amina", "beans", 30), new("Wanjiru", "maize", 55), new("Juma", "maize", 10) })
tests.name: best crop

tests.call: Report.Totals(new List<Harvest> { new("Amina", "maize", 40), new("Juma", "beans", 25), new("Amina", "beans", 30), new("Wanjiru", "maize", 55), new("Juma", "maize", 10) })
tests.name: totals per farmer

tests.why: Use GroupBy for the per-farmer and per-crop totals.

hints: BestCrop: h.GroupBy(x => x.Crop).OrderByDescending(g => g.Sum(x => x.Kg)).ThenBy(g => g.Key).First().Key
Totals: GroupBy farmer, Select(g => new { Name = g.Key, Kg = g.Sum(x => x.Kg) }), sort, then Select($"{t.Name}: {t.Kg}").

exercises.title: Scoreboard questions
exercises.prompt:
Score is given. In static class Board, using LINQ:
- List<string> Top(List<Score> s, int n): "Player:Points" for the best n, highest points first, ties A to Z.
- double AverageOn(List<Score> s, int level): average points of scores on that level, rounded to 1 decimal; 0 if there are none.
- string Status(List<Score> s, int target): "all" if every score reached the target (>=), "some" if at least one did, "none" otherwise (and for an empty list).
- string FirstOver(List<Score> s, int points): the Player of the first score (in list order) with MORE than that many points, or "nobody".

tests.call: Board.Top(new List<Score> { new("Amina", 120, 2), new("Juma", 90, 1), new("Otieno", 120, 3), new("Wanjiru", 40, 1) }, 3)
tests.name: top three

tests.call: Board.AverageOn(new List<Score> { new("Amina", 120, 2), new("Juma", 90, 1), new("Otieno", 120, 3), new("Wanjiru", 40, 1) }, 1)
tests.name: average on a level

tests.call: Board.Status(new List<Score> { new("Amina", 120, 2), new("Juma", 90, 1), new("Otieno", 120, 3), new("Wanjiru", 40, 1) }, 10) + " " + Board.Status(new List<Score> { new("Amina", 120, 2), new("Juma", 90, 1), new("Otieno", 120, 3), new("Wanjiru", 40, 1) }, 50) + " " + Board.Status(new List<Score> { new("Amina", 120, 2), new("Juma", 90, 1), new("Otieno", 120, 3), new("Wanjiru", 40, 1) }, 500)
tests.name: any and all

tests.call: Board.FirstOver(new List<Score> { new("Amina", 120, 2), new("Juma", 90, 1), new("Otieno", 120, 3), new("Wanjiru", 40, 1) }, 100)
tests.name: first over

tests.call: Board.AverageOn(new List<Score> { new("Amina", 120, 2), new("Juma", 90, 1), new("Otieno", 120, 3), new("Wanjiru", 40, 1) }, 9) + " " + Board.FirstOver(new List<Score> { new("Amina", 120, 2), new("Juma", 90, 1), new("Otieno", 120, 3), new("Wanjiru", 40, 1) }, 1000)
tests.name: nothing matches
empty list
tests.hint_if_fail: All(...) is true for an empty list, so check for empty first.

hints: AverageOn: var pts = s.Where(x => x.Level == level).ToList(); if (pts.Count == 0) return 0; return Math.Round(pts.Average(x => x.Points), 1);

exercises.title: Clinic visit summary
exercises.prompt:
Visit is given. In static class ClinicStats, using LINQ:
- List<string> PerClinic(List<Visit> v): "Kisumu: 3" per clinic, most visits first, ties A to Z.
- int BusiestDay(List<Visit> v): the day with the most visits (ties: the earliest day), or -1 if there are no visits.
- List<string> Regulars(List<Visit> v, int minVisits): patients with at least minVisits visits in total (any clinic), each once, A to Z.

tests.call: ClinicStats.PerClinic(new List<Visit> { new("Kisumu", "Amina", 1), new("Kisumu", "Juma", 1), new("Nakuru", "Amina", 2), new("Kisumu", "Otieno", 2), new("Nakuru", "Amina", 2), new("Eldoret", "Juma", 3) })
tests.name: visits per clinic

tests.call: ClinicStats.BusiestDay(new List<Visit> { new("Kisumu", "Amina", 1), new("Kisumu", "Juma", 1), new("Nakuru", "Amina", 2), new("Kisumu", "Otieno", 2), new("Nakuru", "Amina", 2), new("Eldoret", "Juma", 3) })
tests.name: busiest day

tests.call: ClinicStats.Regulars(new List<Visit> { new("Kisumu", "Amina", 1), new("Kisumu", "Juma", 1), new("Nakuru", "Amina", 2), new("Kisumu", "Otieno", 2), new("Nakuru", "Amina", 2), new("Eldoret", "Juma", 3) }, 2)
tests.name: regular patients
a tie goes to the earlier day

tests.call: ClinicStats.Regulars(new List<Visit> { new("Kisumu", "Amina", 1), new("Kisumu", "Juma", 1), new("Nakuru", "Amina", 2), new("Kisumu", "Otieno", 2), new("Nakuru", "Amina", 2), new("Eldoret", "Juma", 3) }, 5)
tests.name: nobody that regular

tests.why: Use GroupBy to count per clinic, per day and per patient.

hints: BusiestDay: if (!v.Any()) return -1; then GroupBy(x => x.Day), order by Count() descending, ThenBy(g => g.Key), First().Key
Regulars: GroupBy(x => x.Patient).Where(g => g.Count() >= minVisits).Select(g => g.Key).OrderBy(n => n)

quiz.q: You sort with .OrderBy(s => s.Level).OrderBy(s => s.Name). What happens?
choices: Only sorted by name: the second OrderBy replaces the first

quiz.why: No items, no average: check first.

quiz.q: After GroupBy(h => h.Farmer), what is g.Key?
choices: The farmer's name for that bucket
quiz.why: Key is what you grouped by.

quiz.q: Why avoid heavy LINQ in Unity's Update()?
choices: It runs every frame and creates garbage that can cause stutters
quiz.why: Plain loops for hot paths; LINQ for reports and menus.

cards.a: list.GroupBy(x => x.Key).Select(g => new { g.Key, Total = g.Sum(x => x.N) })

explain: Explain GroupBy in your own words with an example of a report you'd want from some data you care about.
